prize_parts.citation: For the invention of the optical lattice clock based on magic-wavelength trapping and its development to fractional accuracy and stability at the 10^-18 level.

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B037 to Katori and Ye. The achievement is bounded and identifiable. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice makes the differential light shift of the clock transition vanish while many atoms are held in the Lamb-Dicke regime, and this is the new principle beyond the 2005 comb and the 2012 single-ion control. It is what allows thousands of atoms to be interrogated at once, which is where the stability gain comes from, and it is what led to uncertainties near 1e-18, to many-body effects (collisional and spin-squeezed regimes) that must be controlled and are now exploited, and to centimetre-scale redshift tests and searches for ultralight dark matter and varying constants. Ye's group took strontium to the accuracy and stability frontier and extended it, which is a distinct and well-documented contribution. The round-1 exchange has strengthened the case for me. The two objections that carried weight, Ye's supposed 2005 prize and the pending redefinition of the second, have been answered in the record: Hall and Hansch were the 2005 laureates, and several colleagues (Olsson, Kroll, Danielsson, Johansson) now agree that the redefinition confirms maturity and does not condition it. Five of eight members prefer B037 and no one has described its credit as unresolved. I can judge the systematic-shift physics (polarisabilities, blackbody radiation, higher-order light shifts) from my own work and it is well controlled and independently reproduced.
statement.case_against: The real weakness is novelty and field recurrence. Precision measurement with atoms and lasers was honoured in 2005 and 2012, and a committee could see a further clock prize as one more step on a thread already rewarded. I answer that the lattice scheme is a separate idea, but I accept that the case rests on that one idea and the citation must be narrow. The second weakness is allocation: JILA/NIST, PTB, SYRTE, RIKEN and ion-clock groups (and theorists on magic wavelengths and shifts) are outside the two names, and some of the 1e-18 records are shared among laboratories. I think that is acceptable for a prize built on the invention and its first realisation at record performance, but it is a cost. A third point, raised by Pearce, is that this is an improvement in accuracy and not a new class of matter. I treat that as a difference in what a member values, not as a flaw in the science.

responses.point: Pearce ranks B042 first, regards the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp trio as a defensible compromise despite the omitted Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, and holds that Ye's 2005 association, the pending redefinition and the lack of a new class of matter weigh against B037.
responses.response: I agree that the premise about Ye needs to be withdrawn, as your own summary records, and I appreciate that. On B042 I cannot resolve the credit from outside my field, and I do not want to understate its strength: it has the broadest top-three support, and I keep it as my first alternative. But the experiment tested the BHZ proposal, Zhang cannot be credited later, and the 2016 prize lies nearby, so the trio is a compromise that has to be argued each time. A new class of matter is a strong criterion, but a new capability that rests on a specific physical idea and changes what can be measured also meets the Statutes, and here the idea, the carriers and the reproduction are all clear. Nobody has asked for the redefinition of the second to be awaited as a condition; the demonstrated accuracy does not depend on it.

responses.point: Kroll, ranking B037 first, asks that the citation be written narrowly around the magic-wavelength lattice and the 1e-18 regime, and wants Ye's role stated as clock performance and not only clock-comb integration.
responses.response: I agree and have tightened my citation accordingly: it names the invention based on magic-wavelength trapping and the development to the 1e-18 level, and it does not speak of optical clocks in general. For Ye, the credit I would defend is the demonstrated accuracy, coherence and systematic control of the strontium lattice clock, together with the many-body extensions, and not the comb link, which belongs to the 2005 work. I also accept your point that the adjacent prizes cut both ways; that is why I would put the text of the scientific background, not the citation, in charge of acknowledging NIST, PTB, SYRTE, RIKEN and ion-clock contributors, as Johansson also suggests.

responses.point: Danielsson moved B037 first after the opening exchange but keeps B006 as the more fundamental discovery and says he relies on Kroll's and my reading of the experimental priority history.
responses.response: I welcome the move and will state the priority history plainly: the magic-wavelength proposal and its early demonstration are Katori's, and the accuracy and stability records in strontium are Ye's and several other groups' work, which is why I tie the second name to development and not to the original idea. On B006 I hold to my view: I regard the Higgs observation as the most important unrecognised discovery on the list, but nothing in round 1 offers a principled three-person rule over two collaborations, and Eriksson, Johansson and Kroll reached the same conclusion on the attribution. If someone can show a defensible allocation I will reconsider, but I will not take a proxy for an identification just because the physics is of the highest standing.

responses.point: Eriksson now prefers B042 with a citation on the Z2 prediction and the HgTe observation, concedes the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang asymmetry, and states that as a solid-state theorist he cannot judge the systematic-uncertainty claims of the lattice clock.
responses.response: On the clock, I can give you the assessment you asked for. The systematic budget at 1e-18 (blackbody shift, lattice light shifts including hyperpolarisability, density shifts) is well understood from atomic theory and has been checked between laboratories, so the claim does not rest on one group. As to novelty, the 2005 prize is the comb and the 2012 prize is the control of single trapped ions; neither contains the many-atom, light-shift-free interrogation that defines the lattice clock. On B042, I accept your wording around the Z2 theory plus HgTe as the most honest one, and I would not oppose it, but I still find the BHZ omission a more serious weakness than the two-name limit on B037.

responses.point: Johansson prefers B037 and believes the citation should be narrow, with other lattice-clock and ion-clock work acknowledged in the text and not folded into the prize; he also steps back from B008 because of his own subfield.
responses.response: We agree and I do not think I need to add much. I appreciate that you discount your own interest in B008, which also removes my concern that the committee would be weighing a 2025-adjacent prize. Where I did qualify B029 and B008 in round 1, my concern was timing and credit, not merit, and I would regard either as a worthy later prize. I would not widen the clock credit to the ion or comb groups, since that would blur the attribution that makes the case clean.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept that the magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct principle from the 2005 comb and the 2012 ion control, or insist on reading the three as one thread.
Whether Ye's credit is best worded as accuracy and stability development and whether other laboratories' priority on specific 1e-18 results weakens a two-name prize.
Whether the committee prefers B042 despite the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and Zhang's death problem, and whether I am underweighting a condensed-matter case outside my field.
Whether the mechanism of superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene (B018) is settled enough for a later prize; I keep it as an alternative only.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1. My profile documents a long collaboration with Anne L'Huillier and the Lund group and papers with Ursula Keller's group at ETH Zurich, so I would recuse myself on B004 (Keller) if it came to depth. I work in atomic theory in the same broad field as B037, B016 and B029, but I have no documented tie to Katori or Ye, and no specific conflict on B037. My preferred part and my alternatives (B042, B018) do not involve my documented collaborators.
